bib.title: Language Processing and Python (Chapter 1)
bib.venue: not printed in the chapter PDF

question: What can simple programming with Python and NLTK achieve on large amounts of text, and what are the main challenges of NLP?
contributions: Interactive introduction to NLTK: concordance, similar, dispersion plots, FreqDist, collocations
Python primer on lists, strings, conditionals, loops, list comprehensions
Overview of NLP tasks: WSD, pronoun resolution, MT, dialogue, textual entailment

limits: Authors, year and publisher are not printed in the chapter PDF (only the 'Chapter 1' header and Python 2.4/2.5 era text); bibliographic fields must come from outside.
All code is Python 2.5 / NLTK 2.x era and does not run unchanged on Python 3 / NLTK 3.
Results are illustrative single-run counts on NLTK sample corpora, not experiments with baselines.
Section 1.5 concedes deployed systems cannot do common-sense reasoning or draw on world knowledge robustly.

Dated APIs: print statements (print word, trailing comma); from __future__ import division (default in Python 3); FreqDist.keys() returning list sorted by frequency (now dict-like, use most_common()); fdist.inc(sample) (now fdist[sample]+=1 / update); fdist.max()/N()/freq retained but FreqDist is a Counter subclass; vocabulary1[:50] slicing keys(); bigrams() returns a list (now a generator, wrap in list()); nltk.download() GUI plus 'book' collection; babelize_shell() (Babelfish/Altavista service defunct); the 'L' long-integer suffix; fdist1 < fdist2 comparison operator; text.generate() (removed/limited in NLTK 3); text4.collocations() output format; Python IDLE on MacPython. nltk.clean_html is not in this chapter (appears in ch.3).
practices: Treat text as a list of tokens and measure vocabulary with sorted(set(text)) (1.1, 1.6).
Normalise vocabulary counts by lowercasing and keeping only alphabetic items before counting types (1.4, 1.6).
Skip both very frequent words and hapaxes when looking for characteristic words; combine a length and a frequency condition (1.3).
Use bigram collocations that occur more often than expected from word frequencies, rather than raw frequent bigrams (1.3).
Develop programs in small pieces and test each before combining (1.4).

terms.definition: the technical name for a sequence of characters that we want to treat as a group
the form or spelling of the word independently of its specific occurrences in a text
the set of tokens that a text uses, with duplicates collapsed
len(text) / len(set(text)), the average number of times each type is used
a view of every occurrence of a given word, together with some context
tells us the frequency of each vocabulary item in the text; how the total tokens are distributed across vocabulary items
a word that occurs once only
a word pair extracted from consecutive words of a text
a sequence of words that occur together unusually often, resistant to substitution with similar-sense words
[f(w) for w in text if condition], an idiom that applies an operation to every element
working out which sense of a word was intended in a given context
identifying what a pronoun or noun phrase refers to
identifying how a noun phrase relates to the verb (as agent, patient, instrument, and so on)
automatically pairing up sentences of a document available in two languages
a shared task: decide whether a text provides enough evidence to accept a hypothesis
